preamble: Unrounding of the nasal open-mid front rounded vowel /œ̃/ to /ɛ̃/, merging the two. In Metropolitan French, most speakers in northern France, Paris included, no longer distinguish the /œ̃/ of un, brun and parfum from the /ɛ̃/ of brin, so brun 'brown' and brin 'twig' are homophones. Fougeron & Smith (1993) note that French is traditionally described with four nasal vowels, [ɛ̃ ɑ̃ ɔ̃ œ̃], but that their Parisian speaker, like many others, lacks [œ̃] and uses [ɛ̃] in its place; their transcription has chacun as [ʃakɛ̃] and un voyageur as [ɛ̃ vwajaʒœ]. Wikipedia's Phonological history of French places the merger in the 20th century, when /œ̃/ had a low functional load, and lists Southern France, Switzerland, Belgium, Quebec and Francophone Africa as keeping the contrast. As in the other French cells, the merged vowel is written /ɛ̃/; its Parisian realization is the more open [æ̃]. French /œ̃/ itself goes back to Old French /ỹ/ before a nasal (Latin ūnum > un), through /ø̃/; the atlas has no symbols for those earlier stages.
